clue.text: Coleridge's poem recalled this ruler

indicators.note: recalled is read as called back, so the poem's title is taken in the reverse direction

parts.note: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner is Coleridge's best-known poem

explanation.surface: A ruler is reminded of a Coleridge poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recalled' turns RIME round to give the ruler's title.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim prince, commander or governor, a kind of sovereign.

clue.text: Kit revealing interior to horse

indicators.note: interior to says the revealing word goes inside the word for horse

parts.note: a mare is a female horse
low as in a low-cut neckline, which is revealing

explanation.surface: Something is revealed about the inside of a horse, perhaps by a vet's kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revealing' is the adjective LOW, as in a low-cut dress, not a verb about the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Marlowe, the Elizabethan playwright, was known as Kit.

clue.text: Dick inspired this novel pencil art

indicators.note: novel in the sense of new or fresh signals the letters take a new order

explanation.surface: Philip K. Dick's writing inspired some original pencil drawings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges PENCIL ART. 'Dick' is the author Philip K. Dick, whose androids became the replicants of Blade Runner.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? gave rise to the androids called this in the film Blade Runner.

clue.text: Horses paid to dance in rave

indicators.note: to dance means the letters are set jigging into a new order

explanation.surface: Horses are paid to dance at a rave party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to dance' rearranges HORSES PAID. 'rave' is the verb, to speak with wild enthusiasm.
explanation.definitionFit: To speak or write with extravagant enthusiasm is both to rave and to wax lyrical in this way.

clue.text: Children's author received title character from Baker

parts.note: roger is radio-speak for message received
Miss Hargreaves is the title character of Frank Baker's 1940 comic fantasy novel

explanation.surface: A children's author got a character's name from a baker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baker' is not a tradesman but the novelist Frank Baker, author of Miss Hargreaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Roger Hargreaves wrote and drew the Mr Men books for young readers.

clue.text: Location featuring Red Rum — isn't King extremely eerie?

parts.note: ain't is a colloquial form of isn't
R stands for Rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: extremely asks for the extremes, the first and last letters of the next word

explanation.surface: A question whether a place featuring the racehorse Red Rum, said to be ruled by a king, is very spooky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes E and E from 'eerie'. Red Rum is a famous racehorse that won the Grand National three times.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree, near Liverpool, is the racecourse where the Grand National steeplechase is run, which Red Rum won three times.

clue.text: Auntie often shot adapted Hornby script

indicators.note: adapted means altered, so these letters are rearranged into a new form

explanation.surface: The BBC, nicknamed Auntie, often filmed an adaptation of a Nick Hornby screenplay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adapted' rearranges AUNTIE OFTEN SHOT. Auntie is a British nickname for the BBC, which fits the TV surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick Hornby wrote the short television series of this name about a couple meeting before marriage counselling.

clue.text: Dead sci-fiwriter's incomplete lodge

indicators.note: incomplete says the writer's surname is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: H. G. Wells wrote The War of the Worlds and The Time Machine

explanation.surface: A dead science fiction writer's lodge is left unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incomplete' drops the last S from WELLS to leave WELL.
explanation.definitionFit: To lodge somewhere is to live or reside there, a synonym.

clue.text: I supply cocaine injected by Gothic novelist

indicators.note: injected by means the drug is put inside the novelist's name

parts.note: Bram Stoker wrote Dracula
C is slang shorthand for cocaine

explanation.surface: A drug dealer says the author of Dracula injects the cocaine he supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'injected by' puts C inside STOKER.
explanation.definitionFit: One who keeps a shop's shelves filled is a supplier, and the clue speaks as that person.

clue.text: Leaflets perhaps support a leaderless country

parts.note: a prop is a support

indicators.note: leaderless says the country's name loses its first letter

parts.note: Uganda is an East African country

explanation.surface: Leaflets might back a country with no leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaderless' removes U from UGANDA to leave GANDA.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaflets are an example of political material spread to sway opinion, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Emma's suitor leavingliberal college

indicators.note: leaving, followed by liberal, says the abbreviation for liberal goes out of the suitor's name

parts.note: Mr Elton is the vicar who courts Emma in Jane Austen's novel

explanation.surface: Emma's admirer leaves a liberal college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving liberal' (printed run together) takes L, the usual abbreviation for liberal, out of ELTON. ETON is the English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is the famous English boarding school near Windsor.

clue.text: Plagiarist's work that is in credit

definitions.note: the 's is read as 'is', so the definition is a plagiarist noun

indicators.note: in says the work and the abbreviation go inside the credit abbreviation

parts.note: CR is the accounting abbreviation for credit
op is short for opus, a work
i.e. is the abbreviation for id est, that is

explanation.surface: A plagiarist's work is said to be to his credit.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Plagiarist's' as 'Plagiarist is'; 'work' as OP comes from opus.
explanation.definitionFit: A plagiarist reproduces other people's writing as his own, a synonym for one who imitates.

clue.text: Spare family at Gateshead Hall, for instance

parts.note: the Reeds are Jane Eyre's cruel relatives at Gateshead Hall in Charlotte Bronte's novel
like means such as, for instance

explanation.surface: Spare a thought for the family at Gateshead Hall, for example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spare' looks like a verb, but it is the adjective meaning thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare as in lean and thin, like a slender rush stem.

clue.text: Poet's challenge to engage backward bloke?

definitions.note: the 's is read as 'has', leaving the poet's name as the definition

indicators.note: to engage means to hold within, so the dare encloses the other piece

parts.note: a dare is a challenge

indicators.note: backward says the word for bloke is read right to left

parts.note: a male is a man, a bloke

explanation.surface: A poet challenges someone to take on a backward man.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Poet's' as 'Poet has'. 'backward' gives ELAM, which 'to engage' sets inside the challenge.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter de la Mare was an English poet, author of The Listeners.

clue.text: "If you want a picture of the -, imagine a boot stamping on a human face — for ever" (1984, Orwell)

definitions.text: "If you want a picture of the -, imagine a boot stamping on a human face — for ever" (1984, Orwell)

parts.words: "If you want a picture of the -, imagine a boot stamping on a human face — for ever" (1984, Orwell)
parts.note: O'Brien's chilling line to Winston in Orwell's novel; the missing word is what lies ahead of humanity

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Nineteen Eighty-Four: the missing word is the time to come.
explanation.definitionFit: O'Brien describes what lies ahead under the Party, the time to come.

clue.text: One briefly working lock for Nana?

parts.note: a temp is a temporary worker, employed briefly
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A temporary worker is asked to look after a grandmother's lock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nana' is not a granny but Zola's novel heroine, a courtesan who ruins her lovers.
explanation.definitionFit: Zola's Nana is a seductive courtesan, a woman who lures men.

clue.text: Essayist's very new signature

definitions.note: the 's is read as 'is', leaving the essayist's name as definition

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
a tag is a graffiti artist's signature

explanation.surface: An essayist has a brand new signature.
explanation.walkthrough: A tag is the stylised signature a graffiti artist sprays.
explanation.definitionFit: Susan Sontag was an American essayist, author of Against Interpretation.

clue.text: Husband backing a personal scent over book

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over

indicators.note: backing, set before the three pieces, says they are read from the far end

parts.note: I is the personal pronoun
to dab is to apply scent lightly

explanation.surface: A husband reverses a personal fragrance over a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns A, I and DAB into BADIA. O stands for over in cricket scoring, and the husband comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: Obadiah is the shortest book of the Old Testament, among the minor prophets.

clue.text: Giant man bit into sister whodied

indicators.note: into says the two short pieces go inside the sister's name

parts.note: Beth March, one of the sisters in Little Women, dies
he is a man, by the pronoun
mo is a moment, a bit of time

explanation.surface: A giant man bit into a sister who died.
explanation.walkthrough: Beth is the March sister who dies in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women; 'whodied' is printed run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Behemoth is the huge beast in the Book of Job, so any enormous creature or thing.

clue.text: Snake crossingborder, one where scandal happened

indicators.note: crossing means the snake stretches across, enclosing the other pieces

parts.note: a boa is a constricting snake
a hem is a border on cloth
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A snake slips across a frontier to a place of scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: A Scandal in Bohemia is a Sherlock Holmes story; 'crossingborder' is printed run together, and the snake is the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's story A Scandal in Bohemia names the kingdom as the setting of its scandal.

clue.text: Eliot, initially a friend of Jean Verdenal, waves dramatically

parts.note: T. S. Eliot's initials are T and S
un ami is French for a friend, Verdenal being Eliot's French friend

explanation.surface: Eliot, starting out, was a friend of Jean Verdenal, who waves theatrically.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean Verdenal was Eliot's French friend, to whom Prufrock is dedicated, so his 'a friend' is UN AMI.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsunami is a huge sea surge, a spectacular wall of water.

clue.text: Tiny work in a note Christie carries

indicators.note: carries says the letters are held inside the words in a note Christie

explanation.surface: A small work is held in a note Agatha Christie carries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carries' points to the letters inside 'in a note Christie'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nanotechnology is engineering on the scale of molecules, very small-scale work.

clue.text: English confessor ate this, at first one piece, in utter misery

indicators.note: at first asks for the opening letter of each word that follows

explanation.surface: An English confessor ate this, one piece at a time, in deep wretchedness.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas De Quincey wrote Confessions of an English Opium-Eater; 'at first' takes the first letters of 'one piece in utter misery'.
explanation.definitionFit: De Quincey's Confessions of an English Opium-Eater describes his addiction to the drug laudanum.

clue.text: Fictional ancient city, the setting for 27 books reflecting 27 countries

indicators.note: the setting for says the city surrounds the books, like a setting holding a gem

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Sumerian city
the New Testament has 27 books

indicators.note: reflecting means mirrored, so the two letters are read right to left

parts.note: the European Union has 27 member states

explanation.surface: An ancient city of fiction sets twenty-seven books mirroring twenty-seven nations.
explanation.walkthrough: The 27s are counts: the New Testament has 27 books, the European Union 27 members; 'reflecting' gives UE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fictional story is not factual, a synonym for false.

clue.text: egMarsh fruit

definitions.meaning: Ngaio Marsh, the crime writer, was a New Zealander, nicknamed in this way
a green, furry-skinned fruit also called Chinese gooseberry

explanation.definitionFit: Ngaio Marsh came from New Zealand, whose people share a name with the furry fruit and the flightless bird.

clue.text: Feature of Twilight club flier

parts.note: Stephenie Meyer's Twilight novels feature vampires
a bat is a club, as in cricket or baseball

explanation.surface: Something from the Twilight series flies round a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twilight' looks like dusk, when bats fly, but it is Meyer's vampire series.
explanation.definitionFit: A bat is a flying mammal, and this species feeds on blood.

clue.text: "Dylan, Bob", for example, announced Nobel laureate

indicators.note: announced means the words are spoken, so their sound gives the answer

parts.note: Dylan Thomas is the poet, and Bob is an example of a man's name

explanation.surface: Bob Dylan, a Nobel laureate, is announced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dylan' is not Bob Dylan but Dylan Thomas; 'Bob' is an example of a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Mann, German author of The Magic Mountain, won the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature.

clue.text: No name for smart caveman

indicators.note: no says the abbreviation for name is to be left out of the word for smart

parts.note: to sting is to smart with pain

explanation.surface: A smart caveman goes nameless.
explanation.walkthrough: Stig of the Dump is Clive King's children's book about a caveman found in a chalk pit.
explanation.definitionFit: Stig is the caveman boy in the children's novel Stig of the Dump.
